headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict from shared filesystem/MCP-style workflows; prompt-injection and cascading errors are also plausible.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Claude Code can read repo files and use MCP servers; open-webui supports MCP, plugins, and tool calling. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if one agent writes attacker-controlled text into shared files or tool outputs. The interaction is not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF agent_a writes untrusted content into files that agent_b later parses as instructions
IF agent_b exposes MCP/tool outputs back into agent_a's workspace without provenance checks
mitigations: Restrict shared directories to data-only files
Add a provenance header to any file passed between agents
Disable automatic instruction-following on file contents
Review MCP tool outputs before reuse
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlist parsing

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A handles source code, git history, shell environment, and git credentials; agent B touches documents, notes, API keys, and persistent memory, and both have broad network egress plus file access. If they share a workspace or mounted volume, sensitive material can flow from A into B's uploads or memory, and B can also expose it through external APIs. Defaults are risky.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share any filesystem path or mounted volume
IF agent_b ingests files from the shared workspace into persistent memory or external APIs
mitigations: Separate workspaces and mount points
Remove secrets from the shared directory before either agent runs
Disable persistence for sensitive sessions
Use per-agent API keys with least privilege
requires-engineering: enforce network egress allowlists and DLP scanning

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write files and use broad network egress; agent A also modifies git state, while agent B can operate on local files and mounted volumes in a persistent shared-session architecture. Without explicit locking or isolation, concurrent edits can overwrite each other or corrupt git/workspace state. The profiles show shared-state risk via filesystem and git for A and shared volumes for B.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or mounted volume
IF agent_a commits or rewrites git state while agent_b edits the same files
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories per agent
Serialize write access with a lock file
Pause one agent during git operations
Use separate branches for each agent
requires-engineering: add optimistic-concurrency checks

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can generate code, shell actions, and file edits; agent B can consume files, documents, and tool outputs in a persistent web-app workflow. That makes A's output a plausible upstream input to B, and B may act on it without strong verification. The profiles do not prove automatic action-taking, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF agent_b treats agent_a-produced files or notes as authoritative
IF agent_a writes generated facts that agent_b later renders or forwards without verification
mitigations: Require a human review step before B acts on A's output
Mark A-generated artifacts as untrusted
Add source citations to shared outputs
Compare A's claims against a second source
requires-engineering: implement verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A explicitly handles git credentials and source code on the invoking user's host, while agent B persists prompts, notes, documents, and API keys and can send them to multiple external services. The profiles suggest retention and residency mismatch risk, but they do not establish a specific regulated data class like PHI or EU PII, so medium fits.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into agent_b persistent memory or external connectors
IF agent_a and agent_b are used under different retention or residency policies
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared sessions
Disable long-term memory for sensitive projects
Review connector destinations before use
Use separate tenants or deployments for regulated data
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
